name: UPSC Civil Services (IAS/IPS/IFS)
tagline: India's premier exam for the IAS, IPS, IFS and other Central Civil Services

overview.about: The Civil Services Examination is conducted every year by the Union Public Service Commission to recruit officers for the IAS, IPS, IFS and other Group A and Group B central services. It has three stages — Preliminary (objective, screening), Main (descriptive) and Personality Test (interview). The final merit list is based on 2025 marks: 1750 from Mains and 275 from the interview.
eligibility: Nationality: must be a citizen of India for IAS, IPS and IFS (other services allow certain specified categories — check the notification)
Education: a bachelor's degree from a recognised university; final-year students may appear in Prelims
Age: 21–32 years as on 1 August of the exam year for General/EWS
Age relaxation: OBC +3 years, SC/ST +5 years, PwBD up to +10 years, plus others as notified
Attempts: General/EWS 6, OBC 9, SC/ST unlimited (within age limit); PwBD (General/EWS/OBC) 9
Appearing in either Prelims paper counts as an attempt; always verify the latest UPSC notification

pattern.note: Objective; decides Prelims cut-off; 1/3 negative marking
Qualifying – 25%; language from the Eighth Schedule (exemptions as notified)

pattern.paper: Mains Papers II–V – General Studies I–IV
Mains Papers VI–VII – Optional Subject I & II

overview.frequency: Once a year — Prelims around May/June, Mains around August/September, interviews in the following months

cards.title: Three stages, one rank
cards.body: UPSC CSE is held once a year in three stages: **Prelims** (screening, objective), **Mains** (descriptive, 9 papers) and the **Personality Test** (interview). Prelims marks only decide who reaches Mains. Your final rank comes from Mains written marks plus the interview.
points: Prelims → Mains → Interview
Final merit = 1750 (Mains) + 275 (Interview) = 2025 marks

cards.title: Prelims at a glance
cards.body: Two objective papers on the same day, each 200 marks and 2 hours. **GS Paper I** has 100 questions and decides the cut-off. **Paper II (CSAT)** has 80 questions and is only qualifying, but you must score at least **33%** (66/200). Wrong answers cost one-third of the question's marks.

cards.title: Mains at a glance
cards.body: Nine descriptive papers of 3 hours each. Two are qualifying language papers — **Paper A** (an Eighth Schedule Indian language) and **Paper B** (English), 300 marks each, 25% needed. Seven papers count for merit: **Essay**, **GS I–IV** and **Optional I & II**, 250 marks each = 1750.
points: Essay 250
GS I: Heritage, History, Geography, Society
GS II: Polity, Governance, IR
GS III: Economy, Environment, S&T, Security
GS IV: Ethics
Optional I + II: 500

cards.title: Who can apply
cards.body: You need a bachelor's degree (final-year students may write Prelims). General/EWS candidates must be **21–32 years** on 1 August of the exam year, with **6 attempts**. Relaxations: OBC +3 years and 9 attempts; SC/ST +5 years and unlimited attempts; PwBD up to +10 years.
points: Appearing in even one Prelims paper counts as an attempt

cards.title: Golden rule
cards.body: Always read the latest UPSC notification (usually released in January/February). Rules on age, attempts, service allocation and documents can change, and the notification is the only binding source.

cards.q: What is the total marks on which the UPSC CSE final merit list is prepared?
cards.explain: Mains merit papers (Essay, GS I–IV, two Optionals) = 1750, plus Interview 275 = 2025. Language papers and CSAT are qualifying only.

cards.q: The minimum qualifying score in Prelims Paper II (CSAT) is:
cards.explain: CSAT is qualifying with a 33% minimum (66 out of 200). Only GS Paper I marks decide the Prelims cut-off.

cards.q: How many attempts does a General category candidate get?
cards.explain: General and EWS candidates get 6 attempts; OBC and General/EWS/OBC PwBD get 9; SC/ST are unlimited within the age limit.

cards.title: Why NCERTs first
cards.body: NCERT textbooks (Classes 6–12) explain basics in simple language and are written by subject experts. Many Prelims questions test concepts these books cover. Finishing them first builds the vocabulary you need to understand advanced books and newspapers.
points: Free PDFs at ncert.nic.in/textbook.php

cards.title: Smart NCERT order
cards.body: Read subject by subject, not class by class across all subjects at once. For each subject go from Class 6 upwards so ideas build gradually. Give priority to History, Geography, Polity (Indian Constitution at Work), Economy and Class 11–12 Biology/Chemistry chapters on environment.

cards.title: Then one standard book per subject
cards.body: After NCERTs, pick **one** trusted book per subject and revise it many times instead of reading five. Popular choices among aspirants include Laxmikanth for Polity, Spectrum (Rajiv Ahir) for Modern History, G.C. Leong for Physical Geography and a standard Indian Economy text.
points: One book × many revisions > many books × one reading

cards.title: A 3-read method
cards.body: **Read 1:** understand, no notes. **Read 2:** underline and make short notes or mind-maps. **Read 3:** revise only notes and solve PYQs on that topic. Example: after finishing the Parliament chapter, attempt every Prelims PYQ on Parliament from the last ten years.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Use the official UPSC syllabus as a checklist. Print it, keep it on your desk, and tick topics as you finish them. If a topic is not in the syllabus, do not go deep into it.

cards.q: Which approach is most recommended for static subjects?
options: Read one standard book and revise it several times
Skip NCERTs and start with coaching notes
cards.explain: Repeated revision of one reliable source builds recall far better than a single pass over many books.

cards.q: Where can you download NCERT textbooks free of cost?
cards.explain: NCERT hosts official free PDFs of its textbooks at ncert.nic.in/textbook.php.

cards.title: What Mains tests
cards.body: Mains is not about knowing more facts — it is about presenting them clearly within time. In each GS paper you usually write 20 answers in 3 hours: 10-mark answers (~150 words) and 15-mark answers (~250 words). That is roughly 7–9 minutes per answer.

cards.title: Decode the directive word
cards.body: Every question has a command word. Answer what it asks.
points: **Discuss** – cover various aspects, both sides
**Critically examine** – analyse merits and limits, then judge
**Analyse** – break into parts, show causes and effects
**Comment** – give your opinion backed by evidence
**Elucidate** – explain clearly with examples

cards.title: Intro – Body – Conclusion
cards.body: **Intro (2–3 lines):** define the term, give context, a fact or a recent event. **Body:** sub-headings or points covering every part of the question. **Conclusion (2–3 lines):** balanced, forward-looking, ideally linking to a constitutional value, SDG or government scheme.

cards.title: Mini model
cards.body: Q: 'Discuss the significance of the 73rd Amendment.' Intro: it gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj in 1992. Body: three-tier structure, regular elections, one-third seats for women, finance commission; then challenges like funds, functions, functionaries. Conclusion: true devolution needs the '3Fs' to reach panchayats.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Add value with simple diagrams, flowcharts or a map of India sketch. Quote Articles, committee names, Supreme Court judgments and official data from the Economic Survey. Practise daily and get answers reviewed.

cards.q: For a 15-mark GS Mains answer, the usual word limit is about:
cards.explain: UPSC typically sets ~150 words for 10-mark and ~250 words for 15-mark questions.

cards.q: 'Critically examine' asks you to:
options: Weigh merits and limitations and reach a judgement
cards.explain: Critical examination means a balanced analysis of both sides ending with a reasoned verdict.

cards.title: Static + dynamic
cards.body: UPSC rarely asks pure news. It asks the concept behind the news. If a new tiger reserve is in the news, the question may test the Wildlife (Protection) Act or the Project Tiger history. Always link a news item back to your syllabus topic.

cards.title: Daily routine (60–90 min)
cards.body: Read one national newspaper such as The Hindu or The Indian Express, focusing on editorials, government policy, economy, environment, S&T and international relations. Skip politics gossip, crime and sports results unless they connect to the syllabus.
points: Check PIB for official scheme details
Use PRS for bills and Acts

cards.title: Make notes topic-wise
cards.body: Do not keep notes by date. File each news item under a syllabus heading — 'Polity: Election Commission', 'Economy: Inflation'. Keep short points: what happened, why it matters, related Article/Act, and one data point from an official source.

cards.title: Monthly cycle
cards.body: Week 1–4: daily paper + short notes. End of month: revise one monthly compilation and the Yojana issue. Every 3 months: revise all notes. Before Prelims: revise government schemes, reports and indices from the last 12–18 months.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Prefer official sources for facts — PIB, ministry websites, Economic Survey, Union Budget documents and RBI reports. Many coaching summaries contain errors; verify numbers before memorising them.

cards.q: The best way to organise current affairs notes is:
cards.explain: Topic-wise notes connect news to the syllabus and make revision faster.

cards.q: Which website gives official press releases of the Government of India?
cards.explain: The Press Information Bureau publishes official releases from all ministries.

cards.title: The Constituent Assembly
cards.body: Formed under the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946), the Assembly first met on **9 December 1946**. Dr Rajendra Prasad was its President. On 13 December 1946 Nehru moved the **Objectives Resolution**, which later shaped the Preamble. The Drafting Committee, set up on 29 August 1947, was chaired by **Dr B.R. Ambedkar**.

cards.title: Key dates
points: Adopted: **26 November 1949** (Constitution Day)
Fully in force: **26 January 1950** (Republic Day)
Took about 2 years, 11 months, 18 days
Original: 395 Articles, 22 Parts, 8 Schedules

cards.title: Borrowed features
cards.body: The framers studied many constitutions.
points: UK: parliamentary system, rule of law, single citizenship
USA: Fundamental Rights, judicial review, impeachment of President
Ireland: Directive Principles
Canada: federation with strong Centre, residuary powers with Centre
Former USSR: Fundamental Duties
Government of India Act 1935: much of the administrative framework

cards.title: The Preamble
cards.body: It declares India a **Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic** and promises Justice, Liberty, Equality and Fraternity. The words 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity' were added by the **42nd Amendment (1976)** — the only amendment to the Preamble so far.

cards.title: Is the Preamble part of the Constitution?
cards.body: In **Berubari (1960)** the Supreme Court said no. In **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** it reversed this and held the Preamble **is** part of the Constitution and can be amended, but not in a way that destroys the basic structure. It is not enforceable in courts by itself.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Prelims loves the order of words: 'Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic' and 'Justice – Liberty – Equality – Fraternity'. Remember that 'Republic' means the head of state is elected, not hereditary.

cards.q: Which amendment added 'Socialist' and 'Secular' to the Preamble?
cards.explain: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, added Socialist, Secular and Integrity.

cards.q: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that the Preamble is part of the Constitution?
cards.explain: Kesavananda Bharati overruled the Berubari view and also gave the basic structure doctrine.

cards.q: Who chaired the Drafting Committee of the Constitution?
cards.explain: Dr B.R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee; Rajendra Prasad was President of the Constituent Assembly.

cards.title: Fundamental Rights (Part III)
cards.body: Articles **12–35** guarantee six rights, enforceable in court.
points: Equality (14–18)
Freedom (19–22)
Against exploitation (23–24)
Freedom of religion (25–28)
Cultural & educational (29–30)
Constitutional remedies (32)

cards.title: Article 32 and writs
cards.body: Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution. The Supreme Court (Art 32) and High Courts (Art 226) can issue five writs.
points: Habeas corpus – produce the detained person
Mandamus – 'we command' a public duty
Prohibition – stop a lower court
Certiorari – quash a lower court's order
Quo warranto – 'by what authority' a public office is held

cards.title: Key changes
cards.body: The **44th Amendment (1978)** removed the Right to Property from Part III; it is now a legal right under **Article 300A**. It also ensured Articles **20 and 21** cannot be suspended even during a National Emergency. The **86th Amendment (2002)** added **Article 21A** — free and compulsory education for ages 6–14.

cards.title: Directive Principles (Part IV)
cards.body: Articles **36–51**, inspired by the Irish Constitution, guide the State towards a welfare state — equal pay, living wage, uniform civil code (Art 44), separation of judiciary (Art 50), village panchayats (Art 40). Under **Article 37** they are **not enforceable** in court but are 'fundamental in the governance of the country'.

cards.title: Fundamental Duties (Part IVA)
cards.body: Added by the **42nd Amendment (1976)** on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation, in **Article 51A**. Originally ten; the **86th Amendment (2002)** added the eleventh — parents/guardians must provide education opportunities to children aged 6–14. Duties are non-justiciable.

cards.title: Balance between Parts III and IV
cards.body: In **Minerva Mills (1980)** the Supreme Court held that harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is part of the basic structure. Neither can be given absolute primacy over the other.

cards.q: Which writ is issued to examine the legality of a person's claim to a public office?
cards.explain: Quo warranto ('by what authority') questions the right of a person to hold a public office.

cards.q: Right to Property is now a:
cards.explain: The 44th Amendment (1978) deleted it from Part III and placed it in Article 300A.

cards.q: Fundamental Duties were added on the recommendation of:
cards.explain: The Swaran Singh Committee (1976) led to Part IVA via the 42nd Amendment.

cards.title: Structure
cards.body: Under **Article 79**, Parliament = the **President + Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha**. The President is part of Parliament though not a member of either House, because a bill becomes law only with the President's assent.

cards.title: The two Houses
points: **Lok Sabha:** directly elected, normal term 5 years, maximum strength 550 (after the 104th Amendment ended Anglo-Indian nomination)
**Rajya Sabha:** maximum 250 (238 elected by state/UT legislators + 12 nominated by the President)
Rajya Sabha is permanent — one-third members retire every second year
Vice-President is ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha

cards.title: Money Bill (Art 110)
cards.body: A Money Bill can be introduced only in Lok Sabha with the President's recommendation. The **Speaker** certifies whether a bill is a Money Bill. Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations and must return it within **14 days**; Lok Sabha may accept or reject them.

cards.title: Joint sitting (Art 108)
cards.body: If the two Houses disagree on an ordinary bill, the President can summon a joint sitting, presided over by the **Speaker**. There is **no joint sitting** for Money Bills or Constitutional Amendment Bills. Because Lok Sabha has more members, it usually prevails.

cards.title: Parliamentary tools
points: **Question Hour** – first hour of a sitting
**Zero Hour** – Indian innovation, not in the rules
**No-confidence motion** – only in Lok Sabha, needs 50 members' support to be admitted
**Quorum** – one-tenth of total members
Committees: Public Accounts Committee (chaired by an Opposition member by convention), Estimates, Public Undertakings

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Compare the Houses in a table: who can be dissolved, who passes Money Bills, who can create All-India Services (Rajya Sabha, Art 312), and who can authorise Parliament to legislate on a State List subject (Rajya Sabha, Art 249).

cards.q: Who decides whether a bill is a Money Bill?
cards.explain: Article 110(3): the Speaker's decision is final.

cards.q: A joint sitting of Parliament is NOT possible for:
options: Financial bills other than Money Bills
cards.explain: Article 368 requires each House to pass an amendment separately, so joint sittings are excluded. Money Bills are also excluded.

cards.title: The President
cards.body: Elected indirectly by an electoral college of **elected members of both Houses of Parliament and elected members of State Legislative Assemblies** (including Delhi and Puducherry). Nominated members do not vote. Under **Article 74**, the President acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers; after the 44th Amendment the President may return advice once for reconsideration.

cards.title: Key presidential powers
points: Art 72 – pardon, reprieve, remission, commutation
Art 123 – ordinances when Parliament is not in session
Art 352 – National Emergency
Art 356 – President's Rule in a state
Art 360 – Financial Emergency (never imposed so far)

cards.title: PM and Council of Ministers
cards.body: The President appoints the Prime Minister (Art 75) and other ministers on the PM's advice. The Council is **collectively responsible to Lok Sabha**. The **91st Amendment (2003)** capped the total number of ministers at **15%** of Lok Sabha strength.

cards.title: Supreme Court
cards.body: Established under **Article 124**. Judges retire at **65** (High Court judges at 62). Key Articles:
points: Art 32 – writ jurisdiction for Fundamental Rights
Art 137 – review its own judgments
Art 141 – its law binds all courts
Art 142 – 'complete justice'
Art 143 – advisory opinion to President

cards.title: Appointment of judges
cards.body: Judges are appointed through the **collegium** system that evolved from the Second (1993) and Third (1998) Judges cases. In **2015** the Supreme Court struck down the **National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC)** as violating judicial independence, a basic feature.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Remember: High Courts' writ power (Art 226) is wider than the Supreme Court's (Art 32) — HCs can issue writs for legal rights too, not only Fundamental Rights.

cards.q: The 91st Amendment limited the size of the Council of Ministers to:
cards.explain: Total ministers, including the PM, cannot exceed 15% of the total strength of Lok Sabha.

cards.q: Which Article lets the Supreme Court pass orders for 'complete justice'?
cards.explain: Article 142 empowers the SC to pass any decree or order necessary for complete justice.

cards.q: Who does NOT vote in the Presidential election?
cards.explain: Only elected members take part; nominated members of Parliament and of assemblies are excluded.

cards.title: A 'Union of States'
cards.body: **Article 1** calls India a 'Union of States', meaning states cannot secede. India is federal in structure with a strong Centre — scholars call it 'quasi-federal'. Features: division of powers, written constitution, independent judiciary; but also single citizenship, emergency powers and an appointed Governor.

cards.title: Seventh Schedule
cards.body: Legislative powers are split into three lists.
points: **Union List** – defence, foreign affairs, banking, railways
**State List** – police, public order, public health, agriculture
**Concurrent List** – education, forests, marriage, criminal law
**Residuary powers** rest with Parliament (Art 248)

cards.title: Cooperative federalism bodies
points: Inter-State Council – Article 263
GST Council – Article 279A (101st Amendment, 2016)
Finance Commission – Article 280
NITI Aayog (2015) – created by executive resolution, not constitutional

cards.title: 73rd Amendment – Panchayats
cards.body: Passed in 1992 (in force 1993), it added **Part IX** and the **Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects)**. Three tiers — village, intermediate, district (states under 20 lakh population may skip the middle tier). Five-year terms, **at least one-third seats for women**, SC/ST reservation, State Election Commission and State Finance Commission.

cards.title: 74th Amendment – Municipalities
cards.body: Also 1992, it added **Part IXA** and the **Twelfth Schedule (18 subjects)** for urban local bodies: Nagar Panchayat (transitional area), Municipal Council (smaller urban area) and Municipal Corporation (larger urban area). The idea of three-tier PRIs goes back to the **Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957)**.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Answer-writing hook: local bodies still lack the '3Fs' — Funds, Functions and Functionaries. Use this phrase in GS II answers on decentralisation.

cards.q: The Eleventh Schedule contains how many subjects for Panchayats?
cards.explain: The Eleventh Schedule lists 29 subjects; the Twelfth Schedule (municipalities) lists 18.

cards.q: Residuary powers of legislation in India are with:
cards.explain: Article 248 and Entry 97 of the Union List vest residuary powers in Parliament.

cards.title: Constitutional bodies
cards.body: Created directly by the Constitution, so changing them needs a constitutional amendment.
points: Election Commission – Art 324
UPSC – Art 315
Finance Commission – Art 280
CAG – Art 148
Attorney General – Art 76
National Commission for SCs – Art 338; for STs – Art 338A; for Backward Classes – Art 338B

cards.title: Statutory and executive bodies
points: NHRC – Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993
Central Vigilance Commission – statutory since CVC Act, 2003
Lokpal – Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013
National Green Tribunal – NGT Act, 2010
NITI Aayog – executive resolution, 2015

cards.title: CAG: guardian of the public purse
cards.body: The Comptroller and Auditor General audits accounts of the Union, states and bodies financed by them. Reports on Union accounts go to the President, who places them before Parliament, where the **Public Accounts Committee** examines them. The CAG holds office for 6 years or until age 65.

cards.title: Finance Commission
cards.body: Set up by the President every five years to recommend how central taxes are shared between the Centre and states (vertical devolution) and among states (horizontal devolution). The **16th Finance Commission**, chaired by **Arvind Panagariya**, covers the period 2026–31.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: A favourite Prelims trap: 'NITI Aayog is a constitutional body' — false. It replaced the Planning Commission through a Cabinet resolution in January 2015.

cards.q: Which of these is a constitutional body?
cards.explain: The Finance Commission is created under Article 280. The others are statutory or executive bodies.

cards.q: The National Commission for Backward Classes got constitutional status through:
cards.explain: The 102nd Amendment (2018) inserted Article 338B.

cards.title: From traders to rulers
cards.body: The English East India Company came as traders in 1600. Two battles made it a political power in Bengal.
points: **Plassey (1757):** Robert Clive defeated Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah, helped by Mir Jafar's betrayal
**Buxar (1764):** the Company defeated Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daulah of Awadh and Mughal emperor Shah Alam II
**Treaty of Allahabad (1765):** the Company got the Diwani (revenue rights) of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa

cards.title: Tools of expansion
points: **Subsidiary Alliance** – Lord Wellesley (from 1798): Indian rulers kept British troops at their own cost; Hyderabad was among the first to accept
**Doctrine of Lapse** – Lord Dalhousie: a state without a natural heir was annexed; Satara (1848) was the first, Jhansi and Nagpur followed
Awadh was annexed in 1856 on grounds of 'misgovernance'

cards.title: Land revenue systems
points: **Permanent Settlement (1793)** – Cornwallis; Bengal, Bihar, Orissa; zamindars fixed revenue permanently
**Ryotwari** – Thomas Munro and Alexander Read; Madras and Bombay; direct settlement with peasants
**Mahalwari** – village (mahal) as unit; North-West Provinces, Punjab, parts of central India

cards.title: Economic drain
cards.body: **Dadabhai Naoroji** explained in 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' that India's wealth was being drained to Britain through salaries, pensions, home charges and profits without equal return. This 'Drain Theory' became the core economic critique of colonial rule.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Make a timeline of Governors-General with one signature policy each — Cornwallis (Permanent Settlement), Wellesley (Subsidiary Alliance), Bentinck (abolition of Sati, 1829), Dalhousie (Doctrine of Lapse, railways, telegraph).

cards.q: The Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa was granted to the Company by:
cards.explain: After Buxar, Shah Alam II granted the Diwani through the Treaty of Allahabad in 1765.

cards.q: Which was the first state annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse?
cards.explain: Satara was annexed in 1848. Awadh was annexed in 1856 for alleged misgovernance, not lapse.

cards.title: The Revolt of 1857
cards.body: It began at **Meerut on 10 May 1857**; sepoys marched to Delhi and proclaimed **Bahadur Shah Zafar** emperor. Causes included annexations, heavy revenue demands, social interference and the greased cartridge issue of the Enfield rifle.
points: Delhi – Bahadur Shah Zafar (with General Bakht Khan)
Kanpur – Nana Saheb, Tantia Tope
Lucknow – Begum Hazrat Mahal
Jhansi – Rani Lakshmibai
Bihar (Jagdishpur) – Kunwar Singh

cards.title: Aftermath
cards.body: The **Government of India Act 1858** ended Company rule; power passed to the British Crown. A Secretary of State for India was created, and the Governor-General became the **Viceroy**. Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1858) promised to respect Indian princes and religions.

cards.title: Reformers you must know
points: Raja Ram Mohan Roy – Brahmo Sabha (1828); campaign led to abolition of Sati (1829)
Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar – Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act (1856)
Jyotiba Phule – Satyashodhak Samaj (1873)
Swami Dayanand Saraswati – Arya Samaj (1875)
Swami Vivekananda – Ramakrishna Mission (1897)
Sir Syed Ahmad Khan – Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College, Aligarh (1875)

cards.title: Linking to Mains
cards.body: GS I asks about social reform's role in nationalism. Example line: 'Reform movements spread rational thought, women's education and pride in Indian heritage, preparing the middle class that later led the national movement.' Then give two reformers as evidence.

cards.q: The Revolt of 1857 began at:
cards.explain: The organised outbreak began at Meerut on 10 May 1857 (Mangal Pandey's earlier incident at Barrackpore was in March 1857).

cards.q: Who founded the Satyashodhak Samaj?
cards.explain: Jyotiba Phule founded the Satyashodhak Samaj in 1873 to fight caste discrimination.

cards.title: Birth of the Congress
cards.body: The **Indian National Congress** was founded in **1885** with help from retired civil servant A.O. Hume. Its first session at **Bombay** was presided over by **W.C. Bonnerjee**. The early **Moderates** (Naoroji, Gokhale, Pherozeshah Mehta) used petitions, prayers and protests within constitutional limits.

cards.title: Partition of Bengal and Swadeshi
cards.body: Lord **Curzon** partitioned Bengal in **1905**, officially for administration but in effect to divide Bengali nationalists along religious lines. The response was the **Swadeshi and Boycott movement**. The partition was annulled in **1911**, and the capital shifted from Calcutta to Delhi.

cards.title: Key milestones
points: 1906 – All-India Muslim League founded at Dacca
1907 – Surat Split: Moderates vs Extremists (Lal-Bal-Pal)
1909 – Morley-Minto Reforms introduced separate electorates for Muslims
1916 – Lucknow Pact between Congress and Muslim League; Moderates and Extremists reunited
1916 – Home Rule Leagues of Tilak and Annie Besant

cards.title: Moderates vs Extremists
cards.body: Moderates believed British rule could be reformed and relied on the educated elite. Extremists like Tilak ('Swaraj is my birthright') demanded self-rule and used mass mobilisation, festivals and boycott. Both contributed: Moderates built economic critique; Extremists widened the movement's base.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Prelims frequently asks chronology. Write 1885 → 1905 → 1906 → 1907 → 1909 → 1911 → 1916 on one card and revise it weekly.

cards.q: Separate electorates for Muslims were introduced by:
cards.explain: The Indian Councils Act 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms) introduced separate electorates.

cards.q: Who presided over the first session of the INC?
cards.explain: W.C. Bonnerjee presided over the 1885 Bombay session.

cards.title: Early experiments
points: **Champaran (1917)** – indigo farmers in Bihar; first civil disobedience in India
**Ahmedabad (1918)** – mill workers' strike; Gandhi's hunger strike
**Kheda (1918)** – peasants seeking revenue remission, with Sardar Patel

cards.title: 1919–1922: mass politics
cards.body: The **Rowlatt Act (1919)** allowed detention without trial. On **13 April 1919** General Dyer's troops fired on a peaceful crowd at **Jallianwala Bagh**, Amritsar. The **Non-Cooperation Movement** (1920–22), merged with the Khilafat cause, was withdrawn after violence at **Chauri Chaura** (February 1922).

cards.title: Towards Purna Swaraj
points: 1927 – Simon Commission appointed (no Indian member); 'Simon Go Back'
Dec 1929 – Lahore Session under Nehru demands **Purna Swaraj**
26 Jan 1930 – first 'Independence Day' celebrated
12 Mar–6 Apr 1930 – **Dandi March** starts Civil Disobedience
1931 – Gandhi-Irwin Pact; Gandhi attends Second Round Table Conference
1932 – Poona Pact (Gandhi–Ambedkar) on depressed classes' representation

cards.title: Final phase
points: 1935 – Government of India Act: provincial autonomy
1942 – Cripps Mission fails; **Quit India** resolution on **8 August 1942** in Bombay; 'Do or Die'
1946 – Cabinet Mission; Constituent Assembly elected
3 June 1947 – Mountbatten Plan for partition
15 August 1947 – Independence under the Indian Independence Act 1947

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Link Gandhi's methods to ethics papers too — satyagraha, non-violence and means-ends purity are frequently quoted in GS IV answers.

cards.q: The Non-Cooperation Movement was withdrawn after:
cards.explain: Violence at Chauri Chaura in February 1922, where policemen were killed, led Gandhi to call off the movement.

cards.q: The Purna Swaraj resolution was passed at the Congress session of:
cards.explain: The Lahore Session (December 1929), presided by Jawaharlal Nehru, adopted Purna Swaraj.

cards.q: The Poona Pact (1932) was signed between:
cards.explain: It replaced separate electorates for depressed classes with reserved seats in joint electorates.

cards.title: Harappan Civilisation
cards.body: A Bronze Age urban culture (mature phase roughly 2600–1900 BCE) known for planned cities, grid streets, covered drains and standard weights. Its script is still undeciphered.
points: Harappa (Ravi) – excavated by Daya Ram Sahni, 1921
Mohenjo-daro (Indus) – R.D. Banerji, 1922; Great Bath
Lothal (Gujarat) – dockyard
Dholavira (Gujarat) – water management; UNESCO World Heritage Site (2021)

cards.title: Vedic Age
cards.body: The **Rigveda** is the oldest Veda. The Early Vedic people were mainly pastoral, with assemblies called **sabha** and **samiti**. In the Later Vedic period, agriculture expanded, the varna system became more rigid and kingdoms grew larger.

cards.title: Buddhism and Jainism
points: Gautama Buddha – enlightenment at Bodh Gaya; first sermon at **Sarnath** (Dharmachakra Pravartana); died at Kushinagar
Mahavira – the **24th Tirthankara** of Jainism
Both rejected Vedic ritualism and spoke in people's languages (Pali, Prakrit)

cards.title: Mauryas and Guptas
cards.body: Chandragupta Maurya founded the Mauryan empire; Kautilya's **Arthashastra** discusses statecraft. **Ashoka** turned to Dhamma after the Kalinga war; his edicts are mostly in Prakrit, in **Brahmi** script (Kharosthi in the north-west). The **Gupta age** saw Aryabhata in astronomy and Kalidasa in literature.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Ancient history in Prelims is now mostly culture-linked: Buddhist sites, terms (Tirthankara, Bodhisattva), inscriptions and scripts. Focus on these rather than dynasty lists.

cards.q: Which Harappan site has a dockyard?
cards.explain: Lothal in Gujarat has a structure widely identified as a dockyard.

cards.q: Buddha delivered his first sermon at:
cards.explain: The first sermon was at Sarnath near Varanasi; enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, birth at Lumbini, death at Kushinagar.

cards.title: Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526)
cards.body: Began with **Qutb-ud-din Aibak** and ended when Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi. Five dynasties ruled: Mamluk (Slave), Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi. **Alauddin Khalji** is known for market price control; **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** for token currency and shifting the capital to Daulatabad.

cards.title: The Mughals
points: Babur won the **First Battle of Panipat (1526)**
**Akbar** – mansabdari system, policy of Sulh-i-kul, Ibadat Khana at Fatehpur Sikri
Shah Jahan – Taj Mahal, Red Fort
Aurangzeb – largest territorial extent; reimposed jizya

cards.title: Vijayanagara Empire
cards.body: Founded in **1336** by **Harihara and Bukka**. Under **Krishnadevaraya** it reached its peak; he wrote the Telugu work Amuktamalyada. Its capital Hampi is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The empire declined after the **Battle of Talikota (1565)**.

cards.title: Bhakti and Sufi movements
cards.body: Both stressed personal devotion over ritual and caste.
points: Bhakti: Kabir, Guru Nanak, Mirabai, Tulsidas, Chaitanya; earlier the Alvars and Nayanars in Tamil Nadu
Sufi: Chishti order – Moinuddin Chishti (Ajmer), Nizamuddin Auliya (Delhi)

cards.q: The First Battle of Panipat (1526) was fought between:
cards.explain: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi, ending the Delhi Sultanate and founding Mughal rule.

cards.q: The Vijayanagara Empire was founded by:
cards.explain: Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama dynasty founded it in 1336.

cards.title: Temple architecture styles
points: **Nagara** – North India; curvilinear shikhara (e.g. Khajuraho, Konark)
**Dravida** – South India; pyramidal vimana and large gopurams (e.g. Brihadeeswara, Thanjavur)
**Vesara** – mix of both; Chalukya and Hoysala temples in the Deccan

cards.title: Classical dances
cards.body: The Sangeet Natak Akademi recognises eight classical dance forms.
points: Bharatanatyam – Tamil Nadu
Kathak – North India
Kathakali – Kerala
Mohiniyattam – Kerala
Kuchipudi – Andhra Pradesh
Odissi – Odisha
Manipuri – Manipur
Sattriya – Assam

cards.title: Caves and monuments
points: **Ajanta** – Buddhist caves famous for murals
**Ellora** – Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves; Kailasa temple carved from a single rock under the Rashtrakutas
**Konark Sun Temple** – Odisha, built by Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty, shaped like a chariot

cards.title: UNESCO Intangible Heritage
cards.body: India has several elements on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list, including **Kumbh Mela** (2017), **Durga Puja in Kolkata** (2021) and **Garba of Gujarat** (2023). Tangible sites like Dholavira and Ramappa Temple were inscribed as World Heritage in 2021.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Make a state-wise table: dance, folk art, painting style, major temple. One page per region helps answer both Prelims factual questions and GS I culture questions.

cards.q: Sattriya is a classical dance form of:
cards.explain: Sattriya originated in the Vaishnava monasteries (sattras) of Assam.

cards.q: The Kailasa temple at Ellora was built under which dynasty?
cards.explain: It is attributed to the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I (8th century).

cards.title: Earth's interior
cards.body: The Earth has three main layers: **crust** (thin, rocky), **mantle** (the upper part includes the partly molten asthenosphere) and **core** (iron-nickel; outer core liquid, inner core solid). Much of our knowledge comes from studying earthquake (seismic) waves — S-waves cannot pass through the liquid outer core.

cards.title: Plate tectonics
cards.body: The lithosphere is broken into plates that move over the asthenosphere.
points: Convergent – plates collide; fold mountains like the Himalayas
Divergent – plates separate; mid-ocean ridges
Transform – plates slide past; earthquakes (e.g. San Andreas Fault)

cards.title: Rocks
points: **Igneous** – from cooled magma (granite, basalt)
**Sedimentary** – layered deposits; may contain fossils (sandstone, limestone)
**Metamorphic** – changed by heat/pressure (limestone → marble, shale → slate)

cards.title: Atmosphere layers
points: **Troposphere** – all weather; about 8 km at poles, 18 km at equator
**Stratosphere** – ozone layer; ideal for jet planes
**Mesosphere** – meteors burn up
**Thermosphere** – contains the ionosphere, reflects radio waves
**Exosphere** – outermost

cards.title: Coriolis force
cards.body: Due to Earth's rotation, moving air and water are deflected to the **right in the Northern Hemisphere** and to the **left in the Southern**. The force is **zero at the equator** and maximum at the poles — which is why cyclones do not form right at the equator.

cards.q: The ozone layer is mainly found in the:
cards.explain: Most atmospheric ozone lies in the stratosphere, where it absorbs harmful UV radiation.

cards.q: Marble is a metamorphic form of:
cards.explain: Heat and pressure change limestone into marble.

cards.title: Location
cards.body: India lies entirely in the Northern Hemisphere. The **Tropic of Cancer** passes through eight states: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram. The **Standard Meridian (82°30′E)** passes near Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh.

cards.title: Six physiographic divisions
points: The Himalayas (young fold mountains)
The Northern Plains (alluvial, made by Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra)
The Peninsular Plateau (oldest landmass, part of Gondwana)
The Indian Desert (Thar)
The Coastal Plains (Western and Eastern)
The Islands (Andaman & Nicobar, Lakshadweep)

cards.title: Himalayan vs Peninsular rivers
points: Himalayan rivers are **perennial** (glaciers + rain), form meanders and large deltas
Peninsular rivers are mostly **seasonal** (rain-fed), with shorter, fixed courses
**Godavari** is the largest peninsular river, called 'Dakshin Ganga'
**Narmada** and **Tapi** flow west through rift valleys and form estuaries, not deltas

cards.title: Map practice
cards.body: Take a blank map and mark from north to south: Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra; then Narmada and Tapi (west-flowing) and Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri (east-flowing into the Bay of Bengal). Add one major dam on each. Five minutes daily for a month fixes the map in memory.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: UPSC often asks 'which river is a tributary of which' and 'arrange from north to south'. Learn rivers with their states and tributaries, not in isolation.

cards.q: Which river flows west through a rift valley?
cards.explain: The Narmada (and Tapi) flow west through rift valleys into the Arabian Sea.

cards.q: The Tropic of Cancer does NOT pass through:
cards.explain: It passes through 8 states: Gujarat, Rajasthan, MP, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram — not Odisha.

cards.title: What drives the monsoon
cards.body: The south-west monsoon is a seasonal reversal of winds. Key drivers:
points: Differential heating of land and sea in summer
Northward shift of the **ITCZ** over the Gangetic plain
Heating of the **Tibetan Plateau** and the tropical easterly jet
High pressure east of Madagascar pushing winds towards India

cards.title: Onset and retreat
cards.body: The monsoon normally reaches **Kerala around 1 June** and covers the whole country by early-to-mid July. It withdraws from the north-west from September. During October–December, the **north-east monsoon** brings much of Tamil Nadu's annual rainfall.

cards.title: El Niño, La Niña and IOD
points: **El Niño** – warming of the central/eastern Pacific; often weakens the Indian monsoon
**La Niña** – cooler Pacific; usually supports good monsoon
**Positive Indian Ocean Dipole** – warmer western Indian Ocean; can offset El Niño's effect

cards.title: Local weather terms
points: **Western disturbances** – winter rain in north-west India, good for rabi wheat
**Mango showers** – pre-monsoon rain in Kerala and Karnataka
**Kal Baisakhi** – violent evening thunderstorms in West Bengal
**Loo** – hot, dry summer winds of the northern plains

cards.q: Winter rainfall in Punjab and Haryana is mainly due to:
cards.explain: Western disturbances originate over the Mediterranean region and bring winter rain to north-west India.

cards.q: Tamil Nadu receives a large share of its rainfall during:
cards.explain: The north-east (retreating) monsoon in Oct–Dec gives Tamil Nadu much of its rain.

cards.title: Major soils
points: **Alluvial** – most widespread; Northern Plains; fertile
**Black (regur)** – Deccan basalt; holds moisture; ideal for cotton
**Red and yellow** – iron oxide gives colour; Peninsula
**Laterite** – formed by intense leaching in hot, wet areas; good for cashew, tea, coffee with manure
**Arid** – Rajasthan; sandy, saline

cards.title: Cropping seasons
points: **Kharif** (sown with monsoon, June–July): rice, maize, cotton, soybean, groundnut
**Rabi** (sown Oct–Nov, harvested spring): wheat, mustard, gram, barley
**Zaid** (short summer season): watermelon, cucumber, fodder

cards.title: Minerals and energy
cards.body: Most of India's coal comes from Gondwana coalfields in the **Damodar valley (Jharkhand, West Bengal), Odisha and Chhattisgarh**. Odisha is the leading iron ore producer. Diversifying into solar and wind energy is central to India's climate targets.

cards.title: Green Revolution
cards.body: From the mid-1960s, high-yielding varieties, irrigation, fertilisers and assured prices raised wheat output sharply, especially in Punjab, Haryana and western UP. It made India food-secure but also caused groundwater depletion, soil degradation and regional inequality — a common Mains theme.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Minimum Support Prices are announced by the government on the recommendation of the **Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP)**. Link MSP, procurement and the Public Distribution System when writing on food security.

cards.q: Black soil is best suited for:
cards.explain: Black (regur) soil retains moisture and suits cotton, hence called 'black cotton soil'.

cards.q: Which is a Rabi crop?
cards.explain: Mustard is sown in winter and harvested in spring — a Rabi crop.

cards.title: Measuring output
cards.body: **GDP** is the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a year. **GNP** = GDP + net factor income from abroad. **Real GDP** removes the effect of price changes; **nominal GDP** uses current prices.
points: GDP (expenditure) = C + I + G + (X − M)

cards.title: Key identities
points: GVA at basic prices + product taxes − product subsidies = GDP
NDP = GDP − depreciation
GDP deflator = (Nominal GDP ÷ Real GDP) × 100
Per capita income = National income ÷ population

cards.title: Inflation basics
points: **Demand-pull** – too much money chasing too few goods
**Cost-push** – rising input costs (fuel, wages)
**Stagflation** – high inflation + low growth + unemployment
**Deflation** – sustained fall in general prices
**Disinflation** – inflation still positive but slowing

cards.title: Price indices in India
cards.body: **CPI** (Consumer Price Index), compiled by the National Statistics Office, measures retail prices and is used by RBI for its inflation target. **WPI** (Wholesale Price Index) is compiled by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT, and does not cover services.

cards.title: Inflation targeting
cards.body: Under the amended RBI Act, India follows **flexible inflation targeting** (adopted 2016). The CPI inflation target is **4%** with a tolerance band of **2% to 6%**. If inflation stays outside the band for three consecutive quarters, RBI must explain the reasons to the government.

cards.q: Which index does RBI use for its inflation target?
cards.explain: The target is set in terms of headline CPI (Combined) inflation.

cards.q: GNP is equal to:
options: GDP + net factor income from abroad
cards.explain: GNP adds income earned by residents abroad minus income earned by foreigners in India.

cards.title: Reserve Bank of India
cards.body: Established on **1 April 1935** under the RBI Act 1934 and nationalised in **1949**. It issues currency (except one-rupee notes and coins, issued by the Government), regulates banks, manages foreign exchange and acts as banker to the government.

cards.title: Monetary Policy Committee
cards.body: The **MPC** has **six members** — three from RBI (including the Governor, who has a casting vote) and three appointed by the Central Government. It decides the **policy repo rate** to meet the inflation target while keeping growth in mind.

cards.title: Policy tools
points: **Repo rate** – rate at which RBI lends to banks against securities
**Standing Deposit Facility (SDF)** – floor of the corridor; banks park funds without collateral
**MSF** – emergency borrowing for banks, above repo
**CRR** – share of deposits kept with RBI; earns no interest
**SLR** – share of deposits held in liquid assets like government securities
**Open Market Operations** – buying/selling government securities

cards.title: How a rate cut works
cards.body: RBI cuts repo → banks borrow cheaper → loan rates fall → more spending and investment → growth rises (but inflation may also rise). To fight inflation, RBI does the opposite: raises repo, tightens liquidity.

cards.title: Money supply measures
points: **M0** – reserve money
**M1** – currency with public + demand deposits + other deposits with RBI (narrow money)
**M3** – M1 + time deposits with banks (broad money)

cards.q: Which instrument requires banks to keep cash with RBI without earning interest?
cards.explain: Cash Reserve Ratio balances are held with RBI and earn no interest.

cards.q: How many members does the Monetary Policy Committee have?
cards.explain: Six: three from RBI and three external members appointed by the government.

cards.title: Constitutional basis
points: Art 112 – **Annual Financial Statement** (the 'Budget')
Art 265 – no tax without authority of law
Art 266 – Consolidated Fund and Public Account
Art 267 – Contingency Fund
Art 114 – Appropriation Bill
Art 110 – Money Bill

cards.title: Budget structure
cards.body: The budget has a **revenue account** (taxes, interest, subsidies, salaries — no asset created) and a **capital account** (borrowings, loan recoveries, disinvestment; spending that creates assets or reduces liabilities). Capital expenditure is seen as more growth-friendly.

cards.title: Deficits
points: Revenue deficit = Revenue expenditure − Revenue receipts
Fiscal deficit = Total expenditure − (Revenue receipts + Non-debt capital receipts)
Primary deficit = Fiscal deficit − Interest payments
Fiscal deficit ≈ the government's total borrowing requirement

cards.title: FRBM and GST
cards.body: The **FRBM Act, 2003** sets fiscal discipline goals for the Centre. **GST** was launched on **1 July 2017** after the 101st Amendment, with the GST Council (Art 279A) recommending rates. In September 2025 GST was simplified mainly into two slabs — **5% and 18%** — with a special 40% rate for select luxury and sin goods.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: In Mains, use the Economic Survey and Budget documents on indiabudget.gov.in for official numbers. Quote the source, e.g. 'as per the Economic Survey', instead of approximate figures from memory.

cards.q: Primary deficit is:
cards.explain: Primary deficit removes interest payments, showing borrowing needed for current policies alone.

cards.q: The 'Annual Financial Statement' is mentioned in Article:
cards.explain: Article 112 requires the President to lay the Annual Financial Statement before Parliament.

cards.title: Balance of Payments
cards.body: The BoP records all transactions with the rest of the world.
points: **Current account** – trade in goods, services, remittances, investment income
**Capital account** – FDI, portfolio investment, external loans, NRI deposits
A **current account deficit** must be financed by capital inflows or by drawing down reserves

cards.title: Strengths and weaknesses
cards.body: India usually runs a **merchandise trade deficit** (large imports of crude oil, electronics and gold) but a big **services surplus** (IT and business services). India has been the world's largest recipient of remittances according to World Bank data, which also cushions the current account.

cards.title: Exchange rate and convertibility
cards.body: India follows a **managed float** — market forces set the rupee's value, but RBI intervenes to smooth excess volatility. The rupee has been fully convertible on the **current account since 1994**, but capital account convertibility is only partial.

cards.title: Forex reserves and institutions
points: Reserves include foreign currency assets, gold, SDRs and reserve tranche position in the IMF
**FEMA 1999** replaced the stricter FERA 1973
**WTO** (1995) replaced GATT; India is a founding member
IMF and World Bank were born at Bretton Woods (1944)

cards.title: Depreciation in practice
cards.body: If the rupee moves from ₹80 to ₹85 per dollar, it has depreciated. Exporters earn more rupees per dollar (good for exports), but oil and electronics imports become costlier, which can raise inflation.

cards.q: Which item is part of the capital account of BoP?
cards.explain: FDI is a capital account flow; the others are current account items.

cards.q: FEMA 1999 replaced:
cards.explain: The Foreign Exchange Management Act replaced the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, shifting from control to management.

cards.title: Ecosystem structure
cards.body: An ecosystem has biotic parts (producers, consumers, decomposers) and abiotic parts (light, water, soil). Energy flows **one way** through trophic levels; nutrients cycle. Only about **10%** of energy passes to the next level (Lindeman's ten per cent law).

cards.title: Ecological pyramids
points: Pyramid of **energy** – always upright
Pyramid of **biomass** – can be inverted in oceans (small phytoplankton biomass supports larger zooplankton)
Pyramid of **numbers** – can be inverted, e.g. one tree supporting many insects

cards.title: Key terms
points: **Ecotone** – transition zone between two ecosystems (e.g. mangroves between land and sea)
**Edge effect** – greater diversity in an ecotone
**Keystone species** – has a disproportionate effect on its ecosystem
**Endemic species** – found only in one region

cards.title: Biodiversity hotspots
cards.body: Conservation International identifies **36** hotspots worldwide. India has parts of **four**: the **Himalaya**, **Indo-Burma**, **Western Ghats & Sri Lanka**, and **Sundaland** (which includes the Nicobar Islands).

cards.q: Which ecological pyramid is always upright?
cards.explain: Energy is lost at each trophic level, so the energy pyramid is always upright.

cards.q: Which of these is NOT a biodiversity hotspot covering part of India?
cards.explain: India has parts of Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats & Sri Lanka, and Sundaland.

cards.title: Protected area types
points: **National Park** – highest protection; no grazing or private rights
**Wildlife Sanctuary** – some activities permitted
**Conservation and Community Reserves** – added by the 2002 amendment to the Wildlife Act
**Biosphere Reserve** – core, buffer and transition zones; part of UNESCO's MAB programme when recognised internationally

cards.title: Key laws
points: Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972
Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 — amended in 2023 and renamed Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam
Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 — enacted after the Bhopal gas tragedy
Biological Diversity Act, 2002
National Green Tribunal Act, 2010

cards.title: Flagship programmes
cards.body: **Project Tiger** began in **1973**; the National Tiger Conservation Authority is statutory under the Wildlife Act. **Project Elephant** began in 1992. Cheetahs were reintroduced at **Kuno National Park**, Madhya Pradesh, in 2022 — the first intercontinental translocation of a large carnivore to India.

cards.title: Global conventions
points: **Ramsar** (1971) – wetlands
**CITES** (1973) – trade in endangered species
**CBD** (1992) – biodiversity; Nagoya Protocol on access and benefit sharing
**IUCN Red List** – categories like Critically Endangered, Endangered, Vulnerable

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Protected area counts and Ramsar site numbers change frequently. For Prelims, check the latest figures on the MoEFCC / PIB website a month before the exam rather than relying on older notes.

cards.q: The Environment (Protection) Act was enacted in:
cards.explain: It was passed in 1986 as an umbrella law after the 1984 Bhopal gas tragedy.

cards.q: The Ramsar Convention deals with:
cards.explain: Ramsar (Iran, 1971) is the convention on wetlands of international importance.

cards.title: The science in brief
cards.body: Greenhouse gases — carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and fluorinated gases — trap outgoing heat. Rising concentrations from burning fossil fuels and deforestation are warming the planet, raising sea levels and intensifying heatwaves, floods and droughts.

cards.title: Climate treaty timeline
points: 1992 – **UNFCCC** adopted at the Rio Earth Summit
1997 – **Kyoto Protocol**: binding targets for developed countries
2015 – **Paris Agreement**: keep warming well below 2°C, pursue 1.5°C; every country submits **NDCs**, updated every five years
Principle: **Common But Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR)**

cards.title: India's commitments
cards.body: At COP26 (Glasgow, 2021) India announced **net zero by 2070**. Its updated NDC (2022) aims to cut emissions intensity of GDP by **45%** from 2005 levels by 2030 and to reach about **50%** of installed power capacity from non-fossil sources by 2030 — a share India reported reaching in 2025.

cards.title: Ozone protection
cards.body: The **Montreal Protocol (1987)** phased out ozone-depleting substances like CFCs and is considered the most successful environmental treaty. Its **Kigali Amendment (2016)** targets HFCs — they do not harm ozone but are powerful greenhouse gases.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Indian initiatives worth quoting: International Solar Alliance (launched with France, 2015), Mission LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment), National Action Plan on Climate Change with its national missions, and the Green Hydrogen Mission.

cards.q: The Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol targets:
cards.explain: It phases down hydrofluorocarbons, potent greenhouse gases used in cooling.

cards.q: India's net-zero target year is:
cards.explain: Announced at COP26 in Glasgow, 2021.

cards.title: ISRO milestones
points: ISRO founded in **1969**; Aryabhata (1975) was India's first satellite
**Chandrayaan-3** landed near the lunar south pole on **23 August 2023** — now celebrated as National Space Day
**Aditya-L1** (launched September 2023) studies the Sun from the L1 Lagrange point
**NavIC** – India's regional navigation satellite system

cards.title: Launch vehicles
points: **PSLV** – workhorse for polar/sun-synchronous orbits
**GSLV** – geosynchronous launches with cryogenic upper stage
**LVM3** – heaviest; launched Chandrayaan-3 and is human-rated for Gaganyaan
**SSLV** – small satellites on demand

cards.title: Human spaceflight
cards.body: **Gaganyaan** is India's programme to send astronauts to low Earth orbit on an Indian rocket. In **2025**, IAF Group Captain **Shubhanshu Shukla** flew to the International Space Station on the Axiom-4 mission, becoming the first Indian to visit the ISS.

cards.title: Lagrange points
cards.body: Points where the gravity of two large bodies (Sun and Earth) balances the orbital motion of a small object, so it can stay in position relative to both. **L1**, about 1.5 million km from Earth towards the Sun, gives an uninterrupted view of the Sun — ideal for Aditya-L1.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: For S&T, learn the 'why it matters' of each mission: its objective, the technology it demonstrates and its benefit to India. That gives you material for both Prelims and GS III.

cards.q: Chandrayaan-3's lander touched down near the Moon's:
cards.explain: Vikram landed near the lunar south polar region on 23 August 2023.

cards.q: Aditya-L1 is positioned around L1 because:
options: It is closest to the Moon
It gives a continuous view of the Sun
cards.explain: From L1 the Sun is never blocked by Earth or Moon, allowing continuous observation.

cards.title: Genetic engineering
cards.body: **Recombinant DNA** technology inserts a desired gene into an organism. **CRISPR-Cas9** works like molecular scissors to edit genes precisely; Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it.

cards.title: GM crops in India
cards.body: **Bt cotton** (approved 2002) carries a gene from the bacterium *Bacillus thuringiensis* that makes it resistant to bollworms. It remains the only GM crop approved for commercial cultivation in India. GM crops are cleared by the **Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC)** under MoEFCC.

cards.title: Vaccines
points: Live attenuated – weakened pathogen (e.g. oral polio vaccine)
Inactivated – killed pathogen
Subunit/recombinant – only a protein piece
mRNA – instructs cells to make a viral protein
Viral vector – a harmless virus carries the gene (e.g. Covishield)

cards.title: Emerging tech missions
points: **National Quantum Mission** (approved 2023) – quantum computing, communication, sensing
**IndiaAI Mission** (approved 2024) – compute capacity, datasets, AI startups
**India Semiconductor Mission** – chip fabs and packaging units
**Digital Public Infrastructure** – Aadhaar, UPI, DigiLocker

cards.q: The only GM crop approved for commercial cultivation in India is:
cards.explain: Bt cotton has been commercially grown since 2002; Bt brinjal was put under moratorium in 2010.

cards.q: CRISPR-Cas9 is primarily a tool for:
cards.explain: It edits DNA at precise locations, earning the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

cards.title: Policy frameworks
points: **Neighbourhood First** – priority to South Asian neighbours
**Act East Policy** (2014) – upgraded from the 1991 Look East Policy; focus on ASEAN and Indo-Pacific
**SAGAR** – Security and Growth for All in the Region (Indian Ocean); widened to **MAHASAGAR** in 2025
**Gujral Doctrine** (1996) – non-reciprocal goodwill towards smaller neighbours

cards.title: Regional groupings
points: **SAARC** – founded 1985 at Dhaka; 8 members; largely stalled
**BIMSTEC** – founded 1997; 7 members around the Bay of Bengal; bridges South and South-East Asia
**Indian Ocean Rim Association (IORA)**

cards.title: Water and borders
cards.body: The **Indus Waters Treaty (1960)**, brokered by the World Bank, gave India the eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej) and Pakistan mainly the western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab). India placed the treaty **in abeyance in April 2025** after the Pahalgam terror attack. The **Ganga Water Treaty (1996)** with Bangladesh shares Farakka flows.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: For each neighbour, keep four headings: cooperation (trade, connectivity, energy), irritants (border, water, China factor), recent events, and the way forward. This structure answers almost any GS II neighbourhood question.

cards.q: Which rivers were allocated to India under the Indus Waters Treaty?
cards.explain: The eastern rivers — Ravi, Beas and Sutlej — went to India.

cards.q: India's Act East Policy evolved from:
cards.explain: Look East (1991) was upgraded to Act East in 2014.

cards.title: United Nations
cards.body: Founded in **1945**. The Security Council has **5 permanent members** with veto (USA, UK, France, Russia, China) and 10 elected members for two-year terms. India has served several terms as a non-permanent member and seeks a permanent seat along with reform of the Council.

cards.title: G20 and BRICS
points: India held the **G20 presidency in 2023**; at the New Delhi summit the **African Union** became a permanent member
**BRICS** expanded from 2024 (Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, UAE joined; Indonesia in 2025)
India holds the **BRICS chair in 2026**

cards.title: Other groupings
points: **Quad** – India, USA, Japan, Australia; Indo-Pacific cooperation
**SCO** – India became a full member in 2017
**I2U2** – India, Israel, UAE, USA
**WTO** – trade rules; India pushes for food security and public stockholding

cards.title: Strategic autonomy
cards.body: India buys defence equipment from Russia, partners with the US in the Quad, and works with China in BRICS and SCO. This multi-alignment reflects 'strategic autonomy' — choosing partners issue by issue for national interest, a useful framing in GS II answers.

cards.q: Which body became a permanent member of the G20 during India's 2023 presidency?
cards.explain: The African Union was admitted at the New Delhi Summit in September 2023.

cards.q: Which of these is NOT a Quad member?
cards.explain: The Quad comprises India, USA, Japan and Australia.

cards.title: What GS IV tests
cards.body: GS Paper IV (250 marks) has two parts: **Section A** on theory — ethics, attitude, aptitude, emotional intelligence, thinkers, probity — and **Section B** with **case studies**. It tests your values and decision-making as a future civil servant, not memorised definitions.

cards.title: Ethics, morality, law
points: **Ethics** – systematic principles of right and wrong (often for a group or profession)
**Morality** – personal beliefs about right and wrong
**Law** – rules enforced by the State; something legal may still be unethical

cards.title: Attitude
cards.body: An attitude is a learned tendency to evaluate people, objects or ideas. Its three components (ABC model):
points: **Affective** – feelings
**Behavioural** – actions
**Cognitive** – beliefs and thoughts

cards.title: Emotional intelligence
cards.body: Popularised by **Daniel Goleman**, EI is the ability to understand and manage your own and others' emotions. Five elements: **self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills**. Example: a DM staying calm and empathetic while handling an angry crowd after a flood.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Build a bank of real examples — civil servants, freedom fighters, reformers — for each value: integrity, empathy, courage. One crisp example makes a theory answer stand out.

cards.q: Which is NOT one of Goleman's elements of emotional intelligence?
cards.explain: IQ is cognitive intelligence; Goleman's EI elements are self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skills.

cards.q: The three components of attitude are:
cards.explain: The ABC model: Affective, Behavioural, Cognitive.

cards.title: Foundational values
cards.body: The GS IV syllabus lists the values every civil servant needs:
points: Integrity, impartiality and non-partisanship
Objectivity
Dedication to public service
Empathy, tolerance and compassion towards the weaker sections

cards.title: Nolan Principles
cards.body: The UK Committee on Standards in Public Life (1995) set out seven principles of public life: **Selflessness, Integrity, Objectivity, Accountability, Openness, Honesty and Leadership**. India's **Second ARC** (4th Report, 'Ethics in Governance') drew on similar ideas.

cards.title: Probity in governance
cards.body: Probity means uprightness beyond mere legal compliance. Tools that promote it:
points: Right to Information Act, 2005
Citizen's Charters and grievance redress
Codes of conduct and codes of ethics
Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013
E-governance that reduces discretion

cards.title: Gandhi's Seven Social Sins
cards.body: Published in Young India (1925): politics without principle, wealth without work, pleasure without conscience, knowledge without character, commerce without morality, science without humanity, worship without sacrifice. Very useful for quotes in Essay and GS IV.

cards.q: Which is NOT a Nolan Principle?
cards.explain: The seven are Selflessness, Integrity, Objectivity, Accountability, Openness, Honesty and Leadership.

cards.q: 'Ethics in Governance' is the title of which report of the Second ARC?
cards.explain: The Fourth Report (2007) of the Second Administrative Reforms Commission is 'Ethics in Governance'.

cards.title: A simple framework
points: 1. Identify the **stakeholders**
2. Spot the **ethical dilemma** (e.g. duty vs compassion)
3. List **options** with pros and cons
4. Choose a course and justify it with values and law
5. Suggest long-term systemic fixes

cards.title: Sample case
cards.body: You are a district officer. A contractor close to a local MLA offers a 'gift' and asks you to overlook poor road quality. Stakeholders: public, contractor, MLA, you. Best course: politely refuse, record the offer, order a quality inspection, act per rules and inform superiors. Long term: third-party audits and geo-tagged project monitoring.

cards.title: Ethical lenses
points: **Utilitarianism** (Bentham, Mill) – greatest good of the greatest number
**Kant's deontology** – act on duty; treat people as ends, never merely as means
**Virtue ethics** (Aristotle) – develop good character; the 'golden mean'
**Gandhian** – purity of means and ends; Talisman: think of the poorest person

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Never choose an extreme, illegal or passive option. Examiners reward answers that are lawful, compassionate, practical and that strengthen institutions — not ones that make you a lone hero.

cards.q: 'Act only on that maxim which you can will to become a universal law' is associated with:
cards.explain: This is Kant's categorical imperative.

cards.q: In a case study, the first step should usually be to:
cards.explain: Identifying stakeholders and the core dilemma frames the analysis of options.

cards.title: Why it matters
cards.body: CSAT is qualifying, but you must score 66/200 — and every year some strong GS candidates miss it. Comprehension forms a large share of the paper and is the most reliable way to clear it if you practise regularly.

cards.title: Question types
points: **Main idea / central theme** – what the whole passage argues
**Inference** – what logically follows, though not stated
**Assumption** – unstated premise the author relies on
**Corollary / implication** – a consequence of the argument

cards.title: Method
cards.body: Read the passage once with focus on the author's tone and conclusion. Then read the question and eliminate options that are **too extreme** ('always', 'only'), **outside the passage**, or **true but irrelevant**. Answer from the passage, not from your general knowledge.

cards.title: Mini drill
cards.body: Passage: 'Rising groundwater use for paddy in Punjab is lowering water tables.' Question: the author's assumption? Option 'Paddy needs more water than many alternative crops' is a valid assumption. Option 'Punjab should ban paddy' is too extreme — not assumed.

cards.q: In an inference question, the correct option must be:
options: Supported by the passage even if not stated
cards.explain: Inferences follow logically from the passage without being stated outright.

cards.q: Options containing words like 'always' or 'only' are often:
cards.explain: Absolute words make claims passages rarely support, so treat them with suspicion.

cards.title: Must-know formulas
points: Percentage change = (Change ÷ Original) × 100
Average = Sum ÷ Number of items
Speed = Distance ÷ Time; km/h × 5/18 = m/s
Simple interest = P × R × T ÷ 100
Profit % = (Profit ÷ Cost price) × 100

cards.title: Successive percentages
cards.body: A price rises by 20% and then falls by 20%. Net effect = 20 − 20 + (20 × −20)/100 = **−4%**. So a ₹100 item becomes ₹96, not ₹100.

cards.title: Average speed trap
cards.body: A car goes A→B at 40 km/h and returns at 60 km/h. Average speed is **not** 50. For equal distances use 2xy/(x + y) = (2 × 40 × 60)/100 = **48 km/h**.

cards.title: Ratio sharing
cards.body: ₹1,200 is shared between A and B in the ratio 3:5. Total parts = 8, one part = 150. A gets 3 × 150 = **₹450**, B gets **₹750**.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Do not try every question. In CSAT, aim for accuracy on comprehension and easy quant first, then return to harder items. Remember wrong answers carry a one-third negative mark.

cards.q: A number increases by 10% and then by another 10%. The total increase is:
Convert 72 km/h into m/s.
The average of 4, 8, 12 and 16 is:

cards.title: Common topics
points: Number and letter series
Blood relations
Direction sense
Seating arrangement and puzzles
Syllogisms and statement–conclusion
Clocks, calendars and coding-decoding

cards.title: Series
cards.body: 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ? — differences are 4, 6, 8, 10, so the next difference is 12. Answer: **42**. (Also n × (n + 1): 1×2, 2×3, … 6×7 = 42.)

cards.title: Direction sense
cards.body: Ravi walks 3 km north, turns right and walks 4 km. How far is he from the start? He is 3 km north and 4 km east, so distance = √(3² + 4²) = **5 km**, towards the north-east.

cards.title: Syllogism
cards.body: All pens are books. Some books are bags. Conclusion: 'Some pens are bags'? **Does not follow** — the books that are bags may not include any pens. Draw Venn diagrams to test every possibility.

cards.q: Find the next term: 3, 9, 27, 81, ?
cards.explain: Each term is multiplied by 3: 81 × 3 = 243.

cards.q: A is B's brother. C is A's mother. How is B related to C?
cards.explain: A and B are siblings and C is A's mother, so B is C's child (B's gender is not given).
